title: Achieving an enhanced strength-ductility balance in a 9Cr ferritic-martensitic steel via quenching and partitioning process
abstract: This study investigates the effect of the quenching and partitioning (QP) process on the microstructure and mechanical properties of 9Cr ferritic-martensitic (FM) steel. The results demonstrate that the QP process successfully produces a multiphase microstructure comprising refined lath martensite, metastable retained austenite, and nano-scale precipitates such as Laves phase and M23C6 carbides. The partitioning temperature plays a critical role in microstructural evolution, with increasing temperature leading to a continuous decrease in retained austenite content while inducing non-monotonic variations in martensite block size, low-angle grain boundary fraction, and dislocation density. Under the optimized T400 condition, a favorable strength–ductility synergy is achieved, with an ultimate tensile strength of approximately 1.58 GPa and elongation of 15.3 % at room temperature, and approximately 0.93 GPa with 17.4 % elongation at 600 °C, surpassing the performance of conventional normalized and tempered, oxide dispersion-strengthened, and additively manufactured FM steels. Quantitative strengthening analysis reveals that grain boundary strengthening provides the largest contribution, followed by dislocation strengthening and solid solution strengthening. The transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect from retained austenite significantly enhances ductility, especially in the T400 steel. This study confirms that the QP process represents a viable processing route for achieving excellent strength–ductility combinations in FM steels.
